scenes.heading: The Go Memory Model & Happens-Before
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at the Go memory model and the happens-before relation that defines when one goroutine is guaranteed to see another's writes.

scenes.heading: The central question
items: When is a read guaranteed to see another goroutine's write?
Only when a happens-before edge connects them
No edge means the compiler and CPU may reorder
A data race is undefined behavior
scenes.narration: When two goroutines touch the same memory, the key question is whether a read is guaranteed to see a write. The surprising answer is: only if you synchronize. The memory model defines a partial order called happens-before, and a read sees a write only when the write happens-before it. Without such an edge, the compiler and CPU are free to reorder, and a data race becomes undefined behavior.

scenes.heading: What creates a happens-before edge
steps: A channel send before its receive completes
A mutex Unlock before the next Lock
sync.Once: f completes before any Do returns
An atomic store before a load that sees it
Ordinary reads and writes create NO edge
scenes.narration: Only specific synchronization operations create cross-goroutine edges. A channel send happens-before the corresponding receive completes. An Unlock happens-before the next Lock returns. In sync.Once, the function inside Do completes before any Do call returns. And since Go 1.19, an atomic store happens-before a load that observes it. Plain reads and writes create no ordering at all.

scenes.heading: A channel creates the edge
scenes.narration: This program is race-free precisely because of a happens-before chain. The goroutine writes data, then closes the done channel. The close happens-before the receive in main returns, and the write happens-before the close in program order. Chaining those, the write to data is guaranteed visible when main reads it, so this always prints forty-two — no torn or stale value is possible.

scenes.text: A clean -race run proves nothing about other schedules, and a lone bool flag still needs a sync edge.
scenes.narration: Two dangerous misconceptions. The race detector only reports races on the schedule it actually ran, so a clean pass does not prove your program is race-free on other schedules or hardware. And even a single-word bool flag needs synchronization: without an edge, a reader may see stale data forever or the compiler may eliminate the access entirely.

scenes.text: DRF-SC: race-free programs run sequentially consistent. Racy ones get no guarantees — always synchronize.
scenes.narration: The contract Go formalized in 1.19 is DRF-SC: if your program is data-race-free, it behaves as one sequentially consistent interleaving — the intuitive model. The flip side is that any program with a race gets no guarantees at all. The answer is never to remove synchronization, but to choose the cheapest correct edge.
